title: Night Vision
description: Night vision in night vision cinematography is image intensification: residual photons, and often a near-IR illuminator, amplified through a photocathode and microchannel plate onto a phosphor. The picture is typically green, grainy, blooming around lamps, with the framing of goggles, a weapon sight, or a camera in the dark.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: Someone is hunting or hiding. The world is a tube.
Speculars bloom. Resolution is poor.
Grain is the gain. You are not looking at a graded night exterior.
You are looking through a device that makes the dark usable. Use it as a point of view: a raid, a found camera, a basement with goggles on.
The green (or white phosphor) is the display, not a color grade on a normal sensor. It is the wrong tool for a moonlit scene, for pale IR woods, or for heat outlines.
If trees go white and skies black in clean daylight contrast, that is infrared photography. If bodies are warm masks against cold walls, that is thermal.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Motivate the device: goggles, rifle sight, security cam. High gain, scintillation, blooming highlights, limited dynamic range, maybe a circular or binocular mask, maybe an IR illuminator hot-spot.
Prompt: green phosphor, grainy intensification, surveillance or military eye, blooming lamps, not a teal grade, not thermal.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: A figure on a snow platform seen through goggles, green, noisy, lamps blooming, as a hunter's feed. Do not paint a normal night master green.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: Thermal sees emitted heat, not intensified light. Faces become temperature.
Infrared is a near-IR photograph of reflectance, often in daylight woods. Found Footage is the amateur or diegetic-camera wrapper that night vision often sits inside.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: The Hurt Locker uses intensification as a combat eye. Zero Dark Thirty uses goggle and raid imagery as the operation's seeing.
The Silence of the Lambs puts the audience in night-vision goggles in the dark.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: Wrong cousin: a green color grade, thermal ironbow, or infrared woods. Tell: normal contrast with a hue shift, or heat-colored people, or no grain and no bloom.
Fix: high gain noise, phosphor color, highlight bloom, diegetic device framing.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is night vision in film?
Image intensification of residual light onto a phosphor, usually green and grainy, as goggles, a sight, or a camera in the dark. It is a device look, not a grade.
Night vision vs thermal
Night vision amplifies light. Thermal maps temperature. One blooms lamps and shows a grainy room. The other paints heat and can ignore visible lamps.
When should I use night vision?
When a character or camera is hunting in the dark through a tube. Do not use it as a green wash on a normally exposed night scene.
How do I prompt night vision for AI image or video?
Specify green (or white) phosphor, grain, blooming highlights, and goggle or sight framing. Forbid thermal palettes and ordinary night grades.
